job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Review: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Vulnerabilities

This is based solely on the text you pasted (as amended Oct. 6). It's a drafting analysis, not legal advice. For the markup story, consider having a legislative-drafting or administrative-law expert check the constitutional points (items 27–30).

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "single training run."** A developer could split training into several runs, each under 10^26 operations, through staged pretraining, continued pretraining, or fine-tuning a base model. The total compute could exceed the threshold while no single run does.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A): compute accounting is unspecified.** The bill doesn't say whether compute for synthetic-data generation, reinforcement learning, distillation from a larger model, or failed and restarted runs counts. Without a measurement method, compliance and enforcement both rest on the developer's own accounting.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A): static threshold.** As algorithms become more efficient, more capable models can be trained below 10^26 operations. The bill has no mechanism to adjust the threshold.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) vs. (B): "model" vs. "system."** Prong (A) covers a "model" and prong (B) a "system." A system made of several sub-threshold models (ensembles, agent scaffolds, tool use) escapes (A) unless the Secretary acts under (B).

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B): "the Secretary" is undefined.** The Act never says which Secretary. The Department of Commerce appears only in Sec. 4.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B): vague standard with no procedure.** "Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks" has no criteria, benchmarks, notice-and-comment process, or appeal. Because this definition triggers criminal liability, it invites vagueness and due-process challenges.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B): timing of determinations.** A determination may come only after a system is already trained. The bill doesn't say whether liability reaches back to conduct before the determination, which raises fair-notice problems.

8. **"Artificial intelligence" is undefined.** Both prongs depend on this term, so companies can argue that a given model or system falls outside it.

9. **Sec. 2(2): narrow "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and corporations. It omits lawful permanent residents and non-corporate entities such as LLCs, partnerships, and trusts, which are common structures for AI labs and their subsidiaries.

10. **Sec. 2(2): offshore subsidiaries.** Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies are not U.S. persons. Training conducted abroad through such an entity is likely outside Sec. 3(a), unless a U.S. parent's involvement counts as "develop."

11. **Sec. 2(2): "State" is undefined.** It's unclear whether corporations organized under D.C., territorial, or federal law qualify.

12. **Sec. 2(3): "data center" and "advanced AI chips" are undefined.** There is no chip specification, such as a performance threshold or a reference to export-control classifications, so operators can dispute what counts.

13. **Sec. 2(3): splitting facilities.** Operators can keep each site under 50,000 chips, or train across several smaller data centers, and so avoid registration entirely.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

14. **Sec. 3(a): "train, develop, or deploy" are undefined.** "Develop" could be read broadly, reaching preparatory research, or narrowly. It's also unclear whether a U.S. user accessing a foreign-hosted covered model through an API is "deploying" it.

15. **Sec. 3(a): "in the United States" is undefined.** The text doesn't say whether territories are covered, or whether a U.S.-based person directing training on foreign servers acts "in the United States."

16. **Sec. 3(a): no coverage of model weights.** The bill doesn't address exporting, importing, publishing, or transferring weights of covered or grandfathered models.

17. **Sec. 3(b): broad grandfather clause.** The exemption depends only on training having *begun* before enactment. A company could start a large run just before enactment and continue it indefinitely. The text doesn't say whether fine-tuned or derivative versions of a grandfathered system are also exempt.

18. **Sec. 3(c): open-ended safety exception.** "Activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation" has no definition, approval process, oversight, or limit on scale. A developer could claim that frontier training or deployment serves safety evaluation, and this exception could swallow the rule.

19. **Sec. 3(c): mixed purposes.** The bill doesn't say whether the exception applies when safety evaluation is one purpose among several, such as commercial ones.

## Sec. 4: Registry

20. **Sec. 4: no penalties for registry violations.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing an inaccurate report carries no penalty under this Act, though 18 U.S.C. § 1001 may apply to false statements.

21. **Sec. 4(a): no deadline or process.** No registration deadline is set, and no agency is given authority to issue rules, set report formats, or define what "describing computing workloads" requires.

22. **Sec. 4: no verification authority.** Commerce gets no inspection, audit, or subpoena power. The reports are self-certified.

23. **Sec. 4: "operator" is undefined.** In colocation and cloud arrangements, it's unclear whether the facility owner, the operator, or the tenant running the workload must register and report.

24. **Sec. 4(b): no confidentiality protections.** Reports on workloads may contain trade secrets, and the bill has no FOIA or confidentiality provision. That invites litigation and resistance from companies.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

25. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8: conflicting dates.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. This creates confusion about conduct during that window, and applying the criminal penalty in Sec. 5(b) to that window could raise *Ex Post Facto* problems.

26. **Sec. 3(b) vs. Sec. 8: the 180-day gap.** The grandfather date is enactment, but the effective date is 180 days later. Training begun during that window is not grandfathered, yet the bill doesn't say whether continuing it after the effective date is a violation, or when the violation begins for per-day penalties.

27. **Sec. 5: no enforcing agency or procedure.** The bill doesn't name who assesses civil penalties (Commerce? DOJ through a civil action?), and it provides no administrative process or judicial review.

28. **Sec. 5(a): "each day" is unclear for some activities.** For activities like "develop" and "deploy," it's unclear what counts as a daily violation. Critics may also argue that a $1M daily maximum is small relative to frontier training budgets.

29. **Sec. 5(b): criminal liability on an undefined definition.** "Willfully" offers some protection, but criminal exposure tied to the Secretary's undefined Sec. 2(1)(B) determinations heightens the vagueness and nondelegation concerns in item 6.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

30. **Sec. 6: unclear deadline.** It's unclear whether "not later than 18 months" is a deadline to begin negotiations or to conclude them. The bill also has no reporting requirement, no consequence for missing the deadline, and no definition of "equivalent."

## Sec. 7: Duration

31. **Sec. 7(a): unclear legal effect.** The provision doesn't say whether a congressional finding ends the prohibition automatically. A joint resolution must be presented to the President, so it works much like an ordinary repeal, and Congress could repeal the law anyway.

32. **Sec. 7(a): no instruction to the National Academies.** The National Academies are not directed or funded to produce the report the off-ramp depends on.

33. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b): internal tension.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition "shall remain in effect until" a joint resolution, while (b) ends the whole Act after 10 years. The text doesn't say which controls if no resolution passes.

34. **Sec. 7(b): no savings clause, and an unclear start date.** Nothing preserves pending prosecutions or penalty actions when the sunset arrives, and whether the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) applies to a sunset is debatable. The 10-year clock also runs from enactment rather than the effective date, which shortens the operative period by 180 days.

## Cross-Cutting

35. **No rulemaking authority.** No agency is authorized to issue regulations defining key terms, so gaps must be filled through enforcement and litigation.

36. **No severability clause.** Courts generally presume provisions can be severed, but if 2(1)(B) or the extraterritorial reach of 3(a) were struck down, the bill's text gives no guidance on what survives.

37. **Possible constitutional challenges beyond vagueness.** Opponents may raise First Amendment arguments that code and model weights are protected speech, citing cases like *Bernstein*, and challenge the application to U.S. persons abroad. The strength of these arguments is contested and worth putting to legal experts.

## For Coverage Purposes

Items 18 (safety exception), 17 and 26 (grandfathering and the 180-day window), 20 (an unenforceable registry), and 10 (offshore subsidiaries) are probably the most consequential for whether the bill works as intended. They're good candidates to watch for amendments on Thursday.

If it would be useful, I can draft neutral questions for committee staff or sponsors' offices based on these items.
